Mr. Speaker, Bill C-17, the Insolvency Act, was introduced for first reading in the House of Commons on January 31 of this year. However, the Government has not seen fit since that time to bring forth the Bill for second reading and debate. The only conclusion that I can come to, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government is not giving this Bill high enough priority for active consideration.
Many segments of our society, including the farming community, are counting on this Bill to offer some direction and some relief to individuals who may be on the verge of bankruptcy.
Procrastination by the Government on this Bill has been responsible for many producers going out of business and losing everything that took them years to accomplish. To add insult to injury, it has come to my knowledge from constituents in my riding that some government Members and some staff members of Ministers are spreading untruths and utter falsehoods, to the effect that the Opposition is preventing the passage of the Bill. Mr. Speaker, a crucial factor in Third World development is the work of women. In Africa, 80 per cent of the agricultural work is done by women. In all Third World countries over 50 per cent of the non-imported food is grown by women. In Benin, Burundi, and Liberia, significantly more women are in the labour force than there are men. In Kenya, Lesotho, and Botswana, women head one-third of the families. Actually, over one billion women in Third World countries live in rural areas with agriculture as their primary occupation. In Southeast Asia and West Africa women dominate rural market trade upon which local economies and families are sustained. Third World women have a vital influence on the quality of education, nutrition, and health care.
Cultural patterns in both the North and the South have conditioned people to regard men as the primary movers in economic and social progress. This cultural mind-set has blinded many people to the enormous latent power of women to effect change, if given a helping hand.
At this time the president of CIDA is a woman, Margaret Catley-Carlson. Women are rare in other significant areas of CIDA, however. I suggest that this policy be rescinded and that a far greater emphasis be placed on Canadian women in leadership roles in CIDA programs and projects.
I call on the Government to act on recent OECD guiding principles to aid agencies so that women are brought into decision-making for the design, development, and implementation of projects. Take affirmative action. Place more women in decision-making roles in CIDA. Canada's program could produce much more and better development.

The House resumed from Monday, February 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to review a little of what I said on February 20. Bill C-9 is an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto.
In my opening remarks I began to discuss the notion of what security means in current English. 1 believe there has been a change in the meaning of the word in our part of the world.
During the break we had last week I visited a number of high schools in Saskatoon and spoke to student bodies. I was surprised to find among them a great concern about this Bill. In fact, I received more questions about the security Bill than about any other area of activity in the House of Commons. This was an eye opener to me because I did not realize young people had this concern.
In my opening remarks on the Bill I spoke about the notion of security. Words indicate what is happening in society so the change in the meaning of a word indicate a change in mentality. When I was younger I believed that the word "security" referred to a state of well-being. You were secure when you were in your home; you were well looked after, you were warm, your parents were with you and there was a state of security. In today's world I believe there is an almost completely different understanding of the word, and that is why I think it is important to define what we mean by the word "security" in the Bill.
Today I think security almost means looking at someone as an enemy. To be secure you have to be sure that you can check everybody out. To be secure you have to sort of work against everybody who might be trying to damage your own security. Probably the best example of how the meaning of the word has

March 9, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
changed is with the systems at airports. People now take it for granted that they go through security. They are actually going through a machine which is there because the airline company or society has indicated that everyone in the airport is possibly suspected of subversion. Interestingly enough, no one stands up and protests that what is taking place is an indication to every person that they are actually a security risk and cannot be trusted. 1 feel that change in mentality is something which is very significant in terms of this Bill which is before us.
I have had the experience of living in a part of the world in which there was a radical change in the notion of security. In Latin America in the 1960s the policy which was adopted by five of the major countries there is what is known as the "doctrine of national security". That doctrine began in Brazil in 1964 when the military overthrew the democratically elected Government of Goulart and then put into effect the military regime which has lasted down to the present time, although the severity of that particular regime has tapered off in the last number of years.
Following that takeover there were the coups which took place in Argentina, Uruguay, Chile and Bolivia. Each of them had basically the same mentality and philosophy, which was always based on the idea of national security. National security was understood in the kind of philosophy that one had to be against the enemy and the enemy was, for simplistic purposes, communism. Therefore, the military took over and took away the rights of people. There was no problem at all. There was no discrimination whatsoever. Everyone in a sense became the enemy. Just as Pogo said in the comic strip: "We looked for the enemy and the enemy was us". And that was the factual situation in those countries.
I am not talking about what used to be called "the banana republics". I am talking about countries with high levels of historical democratic process such as Argentina and Chile which had 132 years of democratic governments prior to these takeovers. The reason they were finally taken over was the idea that in those countries there were subversives, communists, people who were going to take over the government, the government having already been taken over by the military. There was this idea that one had to protect oneself against the subversive.
When I learned that the Government was going to introduce a Bill which was based on the idea of having a Security Intelligence Service, I could not believe it. I just could not believe that those kinds of words could be used in Canada. I would like the Government to look seriously at what is happening, because if there is any possibility at all of the philosophy which I have been outlining, under which I have lived and which I have seen operate, taking place right now, I say to government stop, and stop now. Once this kind of operation is in place with its secrecy, there is no way to find out what is happening; and if you happen to be one of the "subversives", there is no way of telling whether your telephone is tapped or your mail is being opened. I have lived through all that. Even
today I have great difficulty feeling really secure that my phone is not being tapped or that my mail is not being opened. That is because I lived for six years where that was a reality in part of the world which not very long before had been a democratic country.
What happened in the situation where everyone became a subversive, and where those countries had to set up a security service not unlike what we have here? It had a body which was the directorship and it had under it the agents. The agents had absolute and total power to do whatever they wanted. Whom did they go after? They went after anyone who questioned what was going on in the government. Who were they? They were the university community.
In the area I lived in Brazil in the 1960s, near the place where I lived, there was a city which had a state university, the city of Maceio. During the period of January, 1969 every single university professor was arrested or detained. Why were they arrested or detained? Because they were subversives? No, because they "might" be subversives. They were questioned and put through police procedures and looked upon as being spies and enemies of the state.
I lived in another reality in which there were a great number of so-called "subversives", people one could not trust. It was the church. People who were actively involved in church responsibilities became the subversives. Many of my friends and colleagues and many of the people I worked with became the subversives. They were arrested and imprisoned and sometimes they were killed. This was all done under the notion of security of the state. Other subversives were the labour unions. Anyone at all who had any influence over the workers, the leaders of the organizations of the workers, became the subversives, the enemies of the state, so they likewise went through the same procedure.
Young people were also involved. They became the enemy because they were asking why this was going on. They asked how it was possible that a government could set up a system which treats its people as though they were all enemies of the state. But it did, and that situation still exists, Mr. Speaker. It exists in several countries yet.
I am happy to say, after having been to Brazil and talked to the human rights people, that much of the early violence against civilians which was carried out by the security services in the name of guarding security has disappeared. However, in Uruguay it still exists. In Chile it is very real. There is no break at all I can see in the position there. Thanks be to goodness, in Argentina I believe there has been a change and that a democratic election has brought back to Argentina- again, a country with a long tradition of working and democratic processes-a system in which it is going back and rechecking that period of its history, the period of violence carried out against its own citizens in the name of justice.
What this Bill is attempting to deal with is the difficult distinction between legitimate dissent and subversion. I admit there are times when that must be a very difficult thing to decide. However, I am very much afraid of the fact that if that is done through a secret system in which the citizens of the
March 9, 1984

country cannot get a responsible answer, it will become very dangerous for the citizens of the country.
What would be considered legitimate dissent? Could it happen down the road that there will be a militant group which will get into government and take over this civilian service? I suspect that that is a real possibility in our country when I observe the ease with which some people, including people in this House, throw around the word "communist" or the word "subversive", and I have heard them use those words. Could it just be down the road that suddenly the same thing will happen and the same kind of people who suffered in Latin America will suffer under this super security mentality, this super necessity to get intelligence and information out of anyone no matter how, whether by using the telephone, the post, or by using prison, intimidation, torture or even death? Is it possible that the beginnings of that kind of mentality in a system is already among us? I speak with emotion about it naturally, because I have lived and suffered under that system.
I ask the Government, and I ask it seriously, to reconsider what it is doing. This notion of setting up a Security Intelligence Service which is not part of the RCMP, which is not something we can question, we can see, talk to and check on to find out what is going on, is a very dangerous precedent in Canadian life.
How did the situation happen in Latin America where there were people who knew about democracy, who had constitutions and well formed governments? I lived through it and I watched it take place. I would like to introduce into the debate today some ideas which have been presented by the Interchurch committee on Human Rights in Latin America. They are ideas which have been put forward by some of the most outstanding theologians, philosophers and historians of Latin America itself, including Jose Comblin, a theologian who is well known throughout all of Latin America and who has written extensively on the church and the national security state in Latin America.
It is claimed that the ideology of the national security state had two main sources. I believe it is true because I have seen it. One might be called indigenous in that it goes back to the roots of Spanish and Italian fascism and those Catholic organizations on the far right involved in all of that. The other can be traced to a much more recent event, the training provided for military and security forces in the U.S. and in the School of the Americas in Panama founded by the U.S., and in the Supreme War College of Brazil. I have spoken to graduates of both places and they have told me about what took place there.
That is where this philosophy, this mentality, was brought forward that you had to have this super security over all citizens so that there would be no subversion, which I agree with, but also that legitimate dissent did not exist. There was no way that you could question what was going on because "big brother", the government, said what is going on is good and you should accept that because "Big Brother" said it is good. There was no way to have legitimate dissent. When
Security Intelligence Service
there was any form of dissent at all from the church, the universities or labour unions, they then became the targets.
What happened next was that, because people could see this was oppression in its worst form, throughout Latin America there was a strong movement among many people, including church people, to have people study in the light of the Gospel and other values whether this was right or wrong. What took place was "conscientization". It is a difficult word, it does not really exist in English, but it is a word-concientizacao- which basically means that people, after studying a reality, grow to a new awareness of who they are and what their rights are under the system they live in. They can have legitimate dissent and speak up and find a better way down the road.
Unfortunately my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and perhaps a question. I was glad the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) mentioned the Interchurch Committee on Human Rights in Latin America because I think it is important to see this whole debate about what constitutes subversion as compared to legitimate dissent in the proper theological and historical context. I ask Members who are genuinely interested in this debate to remember that this debate is at the centre of the very beginning of our civilization, to the extent we call ourselves a civilization based on the Judaeo-Christian tradition.
The central event at the beginning of that tradition, the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, was a matter having everything to do with subversion versus dissent. The crucifixion was a Roman punishment, not a Jewish punishment, for enemies of the state. Christ was regarded as an enemy of the state because He called into question the supremacy of Roman law and Roman authority. He said that people owed their obedience more to the Kingdom of God in its justice than to any temporal or earthly authority. People should keep that in mind and perhaps the Hon. Member would want to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for putting it into very clear religious terms. We are dealing with the essential value of human life and the essential rights of humans. There are different ways of handling that. There is a way of saying that without becoming a criminal. The example of Christ and the crucifixion can be looked on as my colleague demonstrated. There was no way for legitimate dissent against what was going on. You became a subversive and that meant death. His historic example is one that we see many times in modern day life, and death is the answer. I know people who have been killed because they asked questions. I hope this Government looks at the basics and that it will find a way so that our democratic processes and freedoms will be protected without turning us into a police state.

The two schools I speak of are where people were trained to find a way to bring about the total destruction of communism. Now, of course I speak about it in simplicity, but the people who became the communists were the people who were asking questions. They may have been communists, but in my experience the majority of the people were the poor, the oppressed and those who wanted a better deal, a change. But when they started asking for a change they became the subversives. The people who brought about the attack against them, and I have spoken to many of them, have told me that they learned how to do it at either one of those two places.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a final comment. What is being missed as we move from the RCMP to a new civilian security service is the opportunity to have a genuine change in our view of what constitutes subversion. Some of the views which the Member for Saskatoon East expressed about the future are already here. The Government has 800,000 files on Canadians. In 1969 I attended a demonstration at a Liberal fund raising banquet in Winnipeg at which the Prime Minister was speaking in which I protested, a second voyage of the oil tanker Manhattan through the Northwest Passage. I later discovered I was listed as a potential communist because I did not want the Manhattan to go through the Northwest Passage. That is the type of paranoia which has existed in the country at least since 1969-not in the future but since 1969-and which, if we do not change, will lead to the kind of future which the Member for Saskatoon East fears.
Mr. Speaker, I would just say I agree with what the Member said.
Mr. Speaker, there appears to be a kind of love-in with the few remaining socialists in Canada.

I would like to tell the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) that the rights of free speech and dissent are not in the hearts of the NDP alone. It goes back to the axiom that I disagree with everything you say, but will defend to the death your right to say it. I am not quite prepared to go to that length, but Voltaire said that quite some time ago and I do not think he could have been accused of being a socialist. It is true that one must have the right to dissent. I believe all of us on this side of the House certainly believe in that and will sustain it.
This Bill succeeds Bill C-157. It was a feckless, gormless government which produced Bill C-157. At the time of the production of that Bill Canadians were looking for something which would enable us to have a less militant organization, possibly something like the CIA of some years but not of others. We wanted it to be somewhat milder. Instead of that, the Government produced Bill C-157 which would not have
March 9, 1984

given us anything like the CIA. It would have given us something more akin to the KGB. Fortunately the place of sober second thought looked it over and successfully pointed out to the Government that it was a totally inappropriate Bill to be put in front of the Canadian people.
Bill C-9, which is in front of us at the present time, sets up the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. This Bill is somewhat better. It needs a lot of improvement yet and we hope there will be some improvement when it gets into committee. Perhaps it would be useful to the House if I were to discuss this Bill in terms of the organization we have at the present time of which not everyone is aware. It is extraordinarily difficult to get any information on the way the system works at the present time, as everyone knows. I will discuss the organization in those terms first and then review the Bill. This may help us see where we are in danger of going in the future.
The current organization for security and intelligence is amorphous, to say the least. At the present time it does have some component parts which, fortunately, are distributed among several Departments whereby the Ministers can have something to say about what their component is doing. There are three Departments which are quite seriously involved and I think the Solicitor General's Department is first since it controls the RCMP.
As a result of the difficulties in 1970 with the FLQ in Quebec, it was determined there was no crisis management capability in the Government. It was then decided to set up a security section of the RCMP as a result of what happened in those days. At the present time there are sections A, B, D, E, F, H, I, J and L which are operating sections of the security division. I believe these sections are alphabetically designated for functional purposes with certain sections looking after certain problems. One wonders what happened to C, G, and K sections which are missing from their alphabetical list. However, that is a rather specious curiosity.
At that time they decided they should have a civilian in charge of this section of the RCMP. They did not go all the way to choosing a civilian but rather chose Lieutenant General Dare, a very competent and highly qualified military man who had been of considerable assistance during the problems in Quebec at that time. His capabilities had impressed the Government and they made him the head of the security section of the RCMP. I have a great deal of admiration for his capabilities. I do not believe the direction he received was what it should have been.
I will move for the time being from the Solicitor General's Department to the Department of National Defence. There exists the famous section known as the Communications Security Establishment which is located here in Ottawa. It arouses the interest of the media about once a year when someone in the media stumbles over the Communications Security Establishment. We then see a headline such as "Electronic Spy Agency has Doubled in Nine Years". It is difficult to think of anything which has not doubled in nine years, of course. The media immediately interprets it as a great spy agency which is doing something that should not be done. I heard it best
Security Intelligence Service
described as being there to ensure the security of our communications and the insecurity of everyone else's. That may well be the real purpose of the CSE.
It has quite a collection of information for intelligence and other purposes. It does have several sub-parts which are not all that well known. It is useful sometimes in peace-keeping. Under capabilities I would like to mention the electronic surveillance units which they have at the present time. There are very excellent units indeed and the capability of Canadians in electronic surveillance is well known everywhere.
I visited the Sinai desert at the time when Canadian troops were there in a peace-keeping role. As an example of how there can be advantages to this kind of capability, a group had been formed by the United Nations to supervise the green line at that time between the Egyptians primarily and the Israelis. This group which had been established under United Nations supervision had an electronic surveillance capability and possessed some of the most exotic sound detection systems one could imagine. This organization sat on the green line and was able to report not only to the UN or just one side, but to both of the contending sides about what the other side was doing. Everything which they reported was automatically conveyed to both sides. Consequently there was no danger of one side basing its decisions on hearsay information and attacking in a panic situation. Pre-emptive attack is very popular among small countries that get into difficulty and require peace-keeping forces. There was quite some use at that time for surveillance units.
I sometimes disagree with the appropriateness or capability of the RCMP involvement in international espionage when dealing with certain Canadians who occasionally become involved in it. I must confess that the RCMP seems to have a great predilection to turn traitorous Canadians into double agents. As best I can tell, it has a success rate of absolutely zero in this matter. To my knowledge, everyone whom the RCMP has picked off turned out to be too stupid, incapable or had already blown their cover as a double agent.
I would like to refer to a book entitled Men in the Shadows. It mentions that at a certain period of time:
There was a whole new series of successful recruitments in Moscow during the late 1960s and early 1970s. A Canadian corporal acting as chauffeur-assistant to the Canadian Military Attache in Moscow-
As an aside I might note that Canadian military attaches are there to report on the military of the country in which they are stationed. They are not there to open doors for visiting VIPs. They have a duty and are known in the trade usually as bright young officers with good cameras. This one had a chauffeur-assistant who spied for the KGB in the early 1970s. The book goes on to state:
He was apparently caught black-marketing in the exchange of foreign currency and pressured into the role of an agent for which he was rewarded both financially and sexually. He did the usual things, like planting bugs within the embassy and reporting on the weaknesses of other Canadians, and continued to do so after being transferred to Peking. He was discovered by West German Intelligence-

In Bill C-157 we found that there was no real accountability fixed anywhere. Bill C-9 would set up a review committee but neither Bill C-9 nor C-157 provides for the right of the review committee to seek Cabinet documents. I am sure the Cabinet will simply not let the review committee see Cabinet documents. It is interesting to note that the Senate committee recommended that the review committee be allowed to see Cabinet documents. With such a highly sensitive area as this, it is difficult to understand how the review committee could possibly function without that ability.
If one researches to see who is in charge of our present organization, it is the Cabinet Committee on Security and Intelligence. While it has that responsibility, it seems rather loath either to use or accept that responsibility. I recall when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stood in the House and pointed out that in many of these cases it is best that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) not know what was going on. This is a thesis which I cannot accept at all.
I remember the first meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Security and Intelligence when we took office in 1979. We talked to the staff and they told us at that time that it was the first meeting of the committee in two years. To my recollection we had five meetings during the nine months in which we were in office. 1 understand that the committee has met twice in the last year but I do not believe it is really evidence of a reformation on any great scale since it has presumably spent some time studying Bill C-157 and Bill C-9. It would have a difficult time doing that without sitting once in a while.
The make-up of the committee is interesting. When the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) was Prime Minister, he chaired the committee, as does the present Prime Minister. I was the Minister of National Defence and in that role I was the Vice-Chairman of the committee. I notice that now it is the Secretary of State for External Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) who holds that position. This puts External Affairs in a higher position than it was in 1979 as far as this particular committee is concerned.
There are not too many differences in the committee's membership. At that time the Minister of Public Works was on the committee. The present Government has on the committee the Minister of State for Social Development, who is in the other place, as well as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I am not quite sure why these economic Ministers are on the Committee on Security and Intelligence unless they feel that the economy is in such a terrible condition that the whole country might collapse and they will be needed there. I suppose that is for them to decide.
The present Cabinet committee is larger, as is the case with most everything in the Cabinet of the Prime Minister. There
are ten men on their committee and six men on its alternate list. In our day we had seven men and one woman on the committee. I suggest that we should be concerned about the frequency of this committee's meetings.
If we look in the Bill to see who is in charge of this operation, it can be seen that it is quite clearly put into the hands of the Solicitor General. There is no longer any doubt about who is in charge. The definitions clearly put the responsibility on the Solicitor General, far more than it was under the old system when the Cabinet committee had that responsibility. The strange thing that has existed until today-one can understand, knowing that the Cabinet committee practically never met-is that there is a committee of deputy ministers which deals with security and intelligence. It is a committee that does not like to be known as a mirror committee but prefers to be called an interdepartmental committee of deputy ministers. It deals with security and intelligence and has two subcommittees, one on security and one on intelligence.
I have heard from members of that committee of deputy ministers, although General Dare was the person who chaired it, that they have been meeting once a month for four years and corresponding with the Cabinet committee but not receiving any replies. It eventually adopted a strategy of which I do not approve. When it made recommendations or passed resolutions in the committee, it would refer them to the Cabinet committee. If it did not receive a response it would consider that they had been accepted by the Cabinet. This is a very dangerous option for it to practise and I hope this will not take place in the future. When we see the lines of communication provided for in Bill C-9, the Solicitor General has a deputy minister who can report directly to that committee.
The Director of the service will be a very powerful man indeed. He can report either to the deputy minister or to the Solicitor General. But poor people like the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) can only write to the Solicitor General.
And talk to him, too.

He will not be able to send a copy to the person who is making decisions, which would appear to be the Director.

I can say quite frankly I believe there are several hundred military personnel who are involved at the present time in electronic interception. Whether they are going to be converted into civil servants in this organization is not made clear at all. I know we should not be pointing out specific parts of the Bill at this stage of the discussion, but on page 26 of Bill C-9 the RCMP is mentioned very fully. There is no mention made, however, of what will happen to the service personnel.

Mr. Speaker, we are dealing today with a Bill which, if and when enacted, will set up an entirely new security service and lay down the rules and procedures under which this service would operate. Since Canada became a country and up to now, security matters have been left to the RCMP. Most Canadians seem to be satisfied with that. Most Canadian Government and Ministers of Justice or Solicitors General who were supposedly responsible for the administration of the RCMP seemed to be satisfied with that situation.
A few years ago an RCMP officer acting on his own and in his free time in the City of Montreal was injured while placing a bomb on the premises of a private citizen. Because of what

happened he was charged and brought to trial. At his trial he made a number of allegations. He indicated that some RCMP officers had been involved in some highly illegal activities. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) and the present Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) indicated by their replies that they knew very little about what the RCMP had been doing.

Mr. Speaker, during the few minutes I spoke before the noon adjournment, I was listing some of the findings of the McDonald Commission. It found that members of the RCMP had been involved in a number of highly illegal acts, including kidnapping, barn burning, theft of dynamite, the filing of false income tax returns and theft of the membership lists of a legitimate political Party, the Parti Quebecois. 1 am a federalist, Mr. Speaker. I am completely opposed to the major principle behind separatism espoused by the Parti Quebecois, as I am to the principles behind the Canada West party and other groups like it. However, surely as long as individuals, groups or political Parties wish to bring about changes in which they believe in a democratic way, there is no legitimate reason for the security service to be investigating such groups or individuals or to be stealing membership lists, as was done by the RCMP.
Another finding of the McDonald Commission was that the RCMP had files on 800,000 individual Canadians. That is mind-boggling, Mr. Speaker. Some of us have always suspected that the security service of the RCMP had looked into the activities of people involved in the labour movement, some farm organizations, peace organizations, anti-nuclear campaigns and the anti-Cruise campaign, but none of us would
have suspected that the RCMP had accumulated files on
800,000	Canadians. There has been one political assassination in the whole history of Canada. There has been very little in the way of political violence. I have never been able to understand why the security service should be involved in that kind of surveillance.
Some years ago, bowing to pressure of public opinion, Parliament passed an Access to Information Act. Some Canadians were interested in finding out whether the RCMP had files on them and, if so, what those files contained. A number of people, myself included, applied, in the ways which were prescribed under the provisions of that Act, for permission to see our files. This is the kind of response we got from the RCMP, and we got similar responses from the Solicitor General:
In regards to your request concerning our Security Service Records,. . . please be advised that the Governor-in-Council has designated our Security Service Records, described in the Index of Personal Information Banks, as exempt from access under Section 18 of the Privacy Act. We cannot comply with your request nor can we confirm whether or not such information exists concerning you.
That is the kind of reply we get in Canada. I thought that was very interesting because I knew that, using the American freedom of information act in the United States, individuals and organizations had been able to gain access to and acquire copies of information from CIA and FBI Files from the 1960s and 1970s.
I wrote to the Director of the FBI asking to be furnished with a copy of any file which they had on me. I received a reply in January, 1984 acknowledging receipt of my request and indicating that a search of the records would be made to determine if the information I was looking for existed. Then on February 13 I received a letter from the Chief of the Freedom of Information Privacy Acts sections of the FBI which reads as follows:
This is in further response to your Freedom of Information/Privacy Acts ... request. Information pertaining to your request has been set forth below in appropriate paragraphs-
Documents have been located which may pertain to your request and they will be assigned for processing in the near future.
For your information, as a result of the large number of... requests received by the FBI, some delay may be encountered in processing your request.
Just think how ridiculous this situation is, Mr. Speaker. We live in Canada, a middle-sized power with virtually no record of violence, where information about people is being kept secret. The United States is a world power, a country in which Presidents have been assassinated and bombings and shootings have occurred. In the United States, the authorities are quite willing to allow people access to the information which is contained in their files. That is an indication of how seriously the Government of Canada takes the whole question of access to information and how that secrecy impinges upon the right of Canadians to receive the kind of information to which we believe they are entitled.
What do we see in this Bill, Mr. Speaker? The McDonald Commission recommended that the security agency have extensive powers, powers which we think are too great. However, along with those powers, the commission recommended a
March 9, 1984

strong set of controls. Those controls are not contained within this Bill at the present time. As a matter of fact, the first Bill which preceded this Bill met with much hostility. I say to the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis), who seemed to suggest this morning that only members of the NDP were concerned about this Bill, that the first such Bill met with almost unanimous condemnation from civil liberties organizations, Bar Associations and a host of other organizations. Most of the objections which these organizations raised have not really been looked into or dealt with in the present Bill.
The Government has refused to prosecute those RCMP agents who were involved in the illegal activities to which 1 referred earlier. Indeed, the Government has refused to discipline those agents, and in the case of one superintendent, not only was he not prosecuted or disciplined but he received a promotion. We have the idea, which may seem quaint to members of the Government, that if Canadians are expected to be law abiding, as they are, they have the right to expect that all Canadians will abide by the laws, including the members of the security service. Unless all Canadians obey the law, we cannot expect anyone to obey the law.
It is taking the Government too long to bring in legislation designed to create an up-to-date and efficient security service. As I have indicated, the first attempt, Bill C-157, was attacked by lawyers, civil libertarians, trade unions and the provincial Attorneys General. It was so deficient that it had to be withdrawn. That Bill gave the security service authority to open mail and enter premises surreptitiously and it gave the service access to confidential government information without the controls recommended by the McDonald Commission. Allan Borovoy of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association said that under the terms of that Bill as it was formulated, Canadian citizens could have their conversations bugged, their mail opened, their homes surreptitiously searched and their confidential records invaded, even though there was not the slightest suggestion that any law-breaking was involved.

This Bill provides for a Security Intelligence Review Committee comprised of Privy Councillors, former Cabinet Ministers, provincial Premiers or judges. I will not dwell on who the Government may appoint. When one looks at appointments the Government has made in all the fields where it makes appointments, one gets a pretty fair idea of the kind of support and co-operation it expects and gets.
Even this committee, however, will not have access to all documents; Cabinet documents are excluded. Nor does it provide for a review by this committee of the intelligence activities of other Departments. And most important, there is no provision for a parliamentary committee on security and intelligence.
In countries with a larger population than Canada, countries which have much more serious security problems than Canada has-I have mentioned the United States but the same is true of West Germany-parliamentary committees supervise the intelligence activities. There has never been a case where any
Security Intelligence Service
member of the intelligence committee in the United States or West Germany has made public anything which might create difficulties for the security agencies in those countries. There should be a parliamentary committee with the authority to keep records of what the security service in Canada is doing.
The definition of who can be investigated is sadly deficient. People supporting resistance to the Soviet Union's invasion of Afghanistan could be investigated; an organization supporting some of the liberation movements in Africa could be investigated; people supporting the Government of Israel's activities in opposition to certain Arab countries or terrorism could be investigated. We know that in recent years the RCMP has kept under surveillance church groups that have been involved in the kind of activities I have mentioned.
That is false. Church leaders are not under surveillance.
Then who is? Why don't you open the files?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister says that is wrong. The Minister can interject as he has and say that church leaders are not under surveillance. I say to him that there is evidence which has never been denied that people involved in Operation Dismantle were kept under surveillance. I will wait for the Minister to deny that.
God watches us all. God looks out for everyone.

If the Minister does not, it is obvious that he knows that people involved in Operation Dismantle have been kept under surveillance. It is not important whether we agree with the work of the people involved in Operation Dismantle or not; the point is that they are conducting an open campaign in a peaceful way and they ought not to be under the surveillance of any security service.
In the United States telephone tapping, clandestine search or the use of undercover information must have the approval of their Attorney General. That would not be the case in Canada as a result of this legislation. Under this Bill judges determine who will be investigated and how individuals or groups will be investigated. Yet the Attorney General for Ontario, Mr. McMurtry, has described some of the definitions in the Act as being "flabby".
Both in Canada and in the United States a wide variety of legal activities have been investigated. I indicated one example, PQ membership. In the United States the FBI guidelines require that there be a reasonable indication that violence will occur in the not too distant future. This Bill has no such provision. The United States law requires reapplication for permission to wire-tap every 30 days; in Canada the Bill provides for reapplication once a year.
We are not opposed to Canada having a security service. We are not opposed to the security service doing the job it ought to do.

Why not let the Bill go to committee then?

March 9, 1984
Security Intelligence Service

What we are opposed to is the kind of things the RCMP did in past years and which we believe a new security service will do because the Act will make legal the illegal things that were done in the past.
Read the Act.
That is why we oppose the Bill, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a comment. I note that there are some interjections from the Government side of the House, yet not a single Liberal Member other than the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary has been prepared, in four days of debate, to stand and defend the Bill.
You know why. It is because we want the Bill to move to committee. You want it to stay here.
They have refused to defend the Bill because they know what this Bill will do.
You know why we are waiting.

I have spoken.

I am not saying the RCMP security service stole those documents. I do not know. However, it has the documents and refuses to produce them. In very similar situations in the United States, Mr. Speaker, organizations and groups who were investigated and infiltrated by the FBI have used the American Freedom of Information/Privacy Acts and have obtained copies of all the files which that security agency has.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, as I did in my speech, that there is something very sad about a situation in which a world power like the United States can open its files and give information
March 9, 1984

to its citizens, while a country like Canada with so few problems refuses to follow a similar course.

Mr. Speaker, if I may ask the Hon. Member a question, the comments made by his colleague are designed to make the people in the gallery and the people in Burnaby think that somehow or other Hon. Member really believes so.
Look at them laughing.
Mr. Speaker, I wish the Solicitor General would be, first of all, serious-
He is serious.
-and, second, honest. We are dealing with a Bill which arises out of an investigation which took four years and cost millions of dollars.

How many of your Members are going to

That investigation by the royal commission led to a long series of recommendations. It is our contention, Mr. Speaker, and we are supported in this contention by the Civil Liberties Association and many of the Bar Associations and lawyers, that this Bill is somewhat better than the first Bill but it still has major deficiencies.
So let us take it to committee.

I say to the Minister, Mr. Speaker, that if the royal commission which his Government appointed could take four years to investigate and to write a report, then it will not be too bad for the people of Canada if we take another day or two to debate this Bill.

We started in 1969, do you know that?

To say that by keeping this Bill going past closing time today we are trying to destroy this Bill is just not true, and the Minister knows it.

Mr. Speaker, I find the remarks of the Solicitor General and his colleague, the former Minister on the front bench, absolutely incredible. This is one of the most important pieces of legislation we could debate. It has never really been debated in the House of Commons.

You did the same thing on the Crow. On every piece of legislation you do exactly the same thing.

We in the New Democratic Party make no apologies, Mr. Speaker, for not letting the Government get away with things like having 800,000 files on Canadians and opening first-class mail. We are not going to let them railroad the people and we make no apologies.
Thirteen per cent in the last poll and that's where you deserve to be.

One would never know this is a Friday afternoon, Mr. Speaker. I do not question for a moment the sincerity of any of us who say that rather repeatedly.
With respect to Bill C-9, the security intelligence Bill, I do not welcome the opportunity to speak. I am not particularly happy about the Bill. I am very concerned and deeply troubled, Mr. Speaker, and, worst of all, I am very uncertain about this legislation.
There is nothing new about that.

Someone says there is nothing new about that. No, there is not. There have been other Bills with which I have been troubled, concerned and uncertain and, unhappily, I do not have the perfection of my friends from the New Democratic Party and the divine revelation which comes to them with every piece of legislation,

Nor the holiness.
