I believe part of my concern and uncertainty is that this is an extremely important piece of legislation. I would go so far as to suggest that if these times were normal times- by that I mean if they were normal in the economic and social sense, and if we were not in the midst of political events of high priority and high profile-this piece of legislation would have an extraordinary amount of publicity across this country.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: When were times ever normal?

The Minister for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) asks me when were times ever normal. I guess it is like the "ordinary, reasonable man"; it is a piece of fiction. But there are certainly times which approach normality closer than the times in which we now find ourselves.
I suppose that is part of the cause for my concern. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnaty-shyn), put it clearly on the first day of debate when he said that we have "responsibility, as Members of Parliament, to ensure the right balance between national security and the fundamental principles of a free and democratic society". That is a challenge and a serious one. The Minister himself in that same debate, when he opened second reading debate, talked about "the necessary balance between effective national security and the civil liberties which are fundamental to our society".
The seriousness of the challenge is enough for concern, trouble and uncertainty, but I believe my feelings are compounded-and I am trying to put this as kindly as I can, for lack of better words-because I feel we are dealing with tainted legislation. I believe it is tainted in three distinct aspects. One aspect I do not believe is terribly important. It happens to be a fact of political life, and that is the timing of the bill. We all know that in any election year the atmosphere of debate and the approach towards various pieces of legislation takes on an added aura, and that is the election aura. We have seen Bills recently which could be quite legitimately called political bills. They were not substantive in the sense that we regard legislation as substantive; they were political bills. I am not terribly critical. That is a fact of political life. Anyone who has been around here for any length of time will understand that.
However, the two other aspects are much more important with respect to this legislation. They are the history of the legislation and the substance of the legislation and are very much interrelated.
I am happy the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is here because I am speaking very seriously about this. I would like to take a quotation from his speech on second reading as my starting point. He said:
Bill C-9 is the result of a long and difficult process which began 15 years ago.
It certainly has been long and difficult. Without wishing to nit-pick, I quarrel with his word "process". If you use that word in the broad sense, I suppose it has been a process. But I am afraid there has not been any legislative process and that is
part of the problem. What we have had, unhappily-I am not pointing any fingers; I am simply stating what I believe to be an objective view of the facts-is a series of reactions or non-actions. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) interjected a moment ago to the effect that it is 15 years old. Yes, it is 15 years since the Mackenzie report, but that was followed by absolutely nothing. There was no action, not even a reaction. There was absolutely nothing for almost a decade and then the roof fell in.
I remember that well because I had been Solicitor General critic for 11 days when that roof fell in. We remember some very unhappy days in the House during that time which led up to the McDonald Commission. I do not criticize the establishment of that commission; it worked very hard and diligently to produce a very large report. But that was a reaction to the atmosphere in the House after revelation after revelation of alleged wrongdoing. After that commission reported, nothing happened for almost two years. Finally, we had the disaster, unfortunately, of Bill C-157. I do not know who drafted that Bill; I doubt very much the Solicitor General fully appreciated what a mess he was getting himself and the rest of us into with that particular Bill. But again it prompted a reaction, not a process.
Then, Mr. Speaker, a select committee of the Senate was formed. It worked diligently and its report was a damning condemnation. Now we have Bill C-9, a reaction to Senator Pitfield and his colleagues' report from the select committee of the Senate. As I said, it has not been a legislative process as I understand it. A legislative process is nothing more than exercise of government power, which is the right and responsibility to provide a service to the country and its people. It may be a social service, economic or cultural service, or it may be, as in this case, in the field of security.
As I understand the four-step process, Mr. Speaker, the Government examines the need for a new or altered service. That is often triggered by an event, perhaps a dramatic event, or perhaps a cumulative pressure on the Government to do something. It may be a report such as the Mackenzie report, but something happens to trigger that first step. The second step is the Government's diligent examination of the impact or significance of the implementation of the service or change. It may be very minor; a change in a custom's regulation. It could be very major, as I believe is the case with this particular legislation.
The third step is that if there is a major significant impact, then you make sure the public understands it. Before the technical process begins, make sure the public understands it. That can be done in any number of ways, by many vehicles. It could be a discussion or position paper, speeches by the Minister, reference to committee for study; there are all kinds of vehicles to use. I suppose the cliche is: Run it up the flagpole to see if anyone salutes it, or test the waters, or whatever. But it is a very legitimate part of the four-step process. Of course, the final part is to go through the technical process that we find ourselves in now.
March 9, 1984

With respect to the third part, if I can quote the Minister, who I think was dead on when he was talking about the legal framework, he said:
We also believe that such a framework cannot be effective unless we have the support and understanding of the public.
Dead on, Mr. Speaker. I completely concur. Unfortunately,
I do not think the Minister followed his own advice.
Having put it in that four-step context, I hope the Government and the Minister understand what I mean when I say the Bill is tainted. The first step, the examination of the need for a security intelligence service, I suppose was prompted by the Mackenzie Commission, but nothing happened. Nothing really happened after the McDonald Commission for two years. The second step, the examination of significance or impact, was really skipped, unhappily. We certainly did not have the opportunity to discuss it here in the House. The only discussion up until second reading of Bill C-9, I think, was a couple of hours' debate when the Mackenzie report was tabled some 15 years ago. Absolutely nothing has been done to examine publicly the significance or impact of this legislation. Unhappily, Bill C-157 is proof that there was not a diligent and careful examination of the impact of this legislation.
Those steps were ignored, Mr. Speaker, and where does that leave us? Well, we have to deal with this Bill. I am a little concerned because I am quite sure the Minister was not pressing the House to put this Bill into committee fast. He certainly did not say so on February 10. I commend him for that because every Minister likes his Bill to go through the House and into committee. However, I am starting to detect signs of impatience this afternoon. I do not agree with everything the NDP said, far from it, but in 15 years there has not been any real, legitimate debate on the whole area of security and intelligence. Unfortunately, it is compressed into Bill C-9. I say "unfortunately" in all sincerity. It is unfortunate, but it is a fact. The 15 years of legitimate need for debate is compressed into Bill C-9.
That leads me to a very unhappy position, Mr. Speaker. I now regard some of the statements of the Solicitor General with some suspicion, if not cynicism. I am going to use two or three examples. The Minister said:
I am convinced that the mandate described in the Bill amounts to the best possible protection of civil liberties in Canada.
I would really like to be able to say: Yes, I agree. However, I am not in that position, not because of the substantive provisions of the Bill but because of the history, the cloud, changing over this. He then goes on to say:
The Solicitor General will be fully responsible and fully accountable for the security service, as in the present system.
Again I have grave difficulty accepting that statement because I sat here in the pre-McDonald Commission period, as the Solicitor General did although not in that position, and heard more than one Solicitor General deny responsibility. They said: "Oh, that is the day to day operation". Of course the Solicitor General is not responsible for the day to day operations of the RCMP or the security service. Of course not.
Security Intelligence Service
Yes, he is.

But they were so cumulative that they affected the very principle of ministerial responsibility. Therefore, when the Minister makes a statement like the one he made on February 10, given the history of this legislation, how can he with any reasonableness expect me to accept that at face value? I cannot do it because the history leading up to Bill C-9 does not permit me to do that.
Finally, we have the statement:
The Review Committee will have full access to detailed information on the activities of the service.
We are talking about accountability. I have to say to the Minister that if there is to be accountability, it has to be complete. There is no such thing as being half accountable or partially accountable or even 99 per cent accountable. Unless it is complete accountability, there is no such thing. Unless those Cabinet documents in the possession of the security service are opened to the Inspector General, and through him to the Review Committee, I say there is not accountability. Those documents in the possession of the security service, even though they are classified as a Cabinet document, are likely the most vital documents relating to accountability.
As a result of this it will be heavy going in the committee. However, we have had committees before which were heavy going. I think the Minister and his colleagues on the Treasury benches have to be very flexible about this. I do not think there is any way to avoid giving this committee permission to travel. The historic element, the separation of the proposed force from the traditional RCMP force, dictates that necessity. Given the chequered career that this legislation has had, I see no way around that at all.
I believe it was either the Minister or my colleague for Saskatoon West who spoke about the morale of the force. I am concerned about that, as I think we all should be. While the principle of upholding the morale within the RCMP security intelligence branch is important, it is not as important as the principles of civil liberties and the security of the country. Therefore, while that morale may continue to suffer because of the 15 long and difficult years, I regret it very much but there are other principles which I believe are paramount to that. Those are the principles of the protection of our rights as citizens and the protection of the integrity of our country from those who would seek to attack it. I wish I had more time to deal with the mandate and powers; I know I have not.
Before the Speaker cuts me off, I would like to say that my principal concern is accountability. The Minister has made significant changes from Bill C-157. I am speaking about changes with respect to the operation and powers of the Director. I am a little concerned because the Bill does not correspond with the Senate committee report. I am concerned about the provision that the Minister may issue written directions to the Director. What about oral directions? Should all directions not be in writing? Would this provision create an

March 9, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
incentive for the Solicitor General not to reduce his directions to writing? If that became the case I would be concerned.
I am concerned about the establishment of the office of the Inspector General. Unless the Solicitor General follows the recommendations of the Senate committee which would allow the Inspector General access to Cabinet documents within the possession of the security service, accountability sadly suffers. Unless the accountability is 100 per cent, I do not believe it amounts to anything. The Inspector General would be deprived of the directives and documents of a Cabinet nature which he gets from his political superiors, which I believe is most important.
Finally, unless the Inspector General has access to those particular Cabinet documents, the review committee will not. My comments with respect to the Inspector General apply equally, and possibly with greater force, to the review committee.
With respect to the make-up of the review committee, I am not sure whether it is better to have Privy Councillors as compared to those who are now serving in either the House or Senate. I believe the recommended number is three to five Members. I doubt that that is large enough; it may be. The Senate committee in the United States has reasonably good sized membership composed of very senior and prestigious senators in that country. It is very prestigious in the sense that you are judged by your peers to be privy to highly confidential information.
I presume my time is just about up. I have no particular comment to make at the second reading stage with respect to the make-up of that review committee. I think that is something we could deal with in committee. I believe committee stage is absolutely crucial if the Bill is to be rescued. I believe it should be. I believe there should be a security service, either inside the RCMP or outside. The committee stage is going to be absolutely crucial to that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. He has referred to the work of both the Inspector General and the review committee. Does the Hon. Member think it would be important or useful for either of those agencies to have the right, if it is felt necessary, to make public their questions and findings if they find the security service has acted improperly, as the McDonald Commission found the security service of the RCMP had done in earlier years?

Mr. Speaker, I believe I read the Bill carefully. I thought there was a provision for the review committee to report to Parliament at least annually, if not more often. I support that reporting principle.
Perhaps the Hon. Member's question is a little broader than that. If a particular incident occurs, should or could the review committee make it public? I would agree to that subject to it not threatening or putting in danger the security of the state.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone would want any information to get out which would endanger security. However, if the Inspector General and the review committee are bound by the oath of secrecy, all they will be able to do is report to the Solicitor General. The Solicitor General can then decide whether to take action. We know from past experience that if Solicitors General knew what was going on they were, to say the least, loath to do anything about it. Surely the right of both of these groups to make public the type of situation which had occurred, although not necessarily the specific details of the act, in order for corrective action to be taken would be a necessary part of an Act which will do the job we want it to do.

Mr. Speaker, there are two report clauses, Clauses 52 and 53. Clause 54 is a special report section. I would have to read them carefully to discover whether they address the concerns of the Hon. Member. I notice one report must be laid before Parliament on any of the first 15 days on which the House is sitting after the Minister receives it. I do not know whether that will address his particular concern. There are four or five clauses dealing with reports so I really cannot be any more specific than that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment with respect to the last point which was made by the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis). The Member is quite correct that there is provision in the legislation for reporting to Parliament. The difficulty with that, as was pointed out by my colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), is that before this report is tabled in Parliament the Inspector General of the civilian security servie must vet the report. It is up to the Inspector General to go through that report with a finetoothed comb and ensure that in no way is the oath of secrecy of the members of the Security Intelligence Review Committee in any way breached. Therefore, the only document which could possibly come before the House would be a document so meaningless and devoid of any content that it would not be able to draw attention to any wrongdoing which had been identified.
Perhaps I can ask the Hon. Member a question and then he could comment. The McDonald Commission strongly recommended the establishment of a parliamentary oversight committee, made up of Members on all sides of the House, which would have full access to all of the documentation and the budget of the new civilian security service.
Similar committees are in existence in the Senate and the House of Representatives in the United States, in West Germany and elsewhere. The Hon. Member has considerable experience in this area and I know that he is a former spokesperson for his Party on justice and is an active member of the Justice Committee. I would be most interested to hear his views with respect to this very sensible suggestion of the McDonald Commission. It is a suggestion which unfortunately has been rejected in this Bill.

With respect to the comment about the fact that the report would be meaningless or have nothing in it, to use
March 9, 1984

the Hon. Member's words, I am not so sure that I would be so quick to prejudge what that type of report would be. I am quite prepared to discuss and debate that in committee, which 1 believe is the place to do it. My opinion is quite flexible in that respect.
With respect to his second point, it is quite difficult to say who should be the watcher of watchers. The Minister proposes a committee of Privy Councillors. On the other hand, it was proposed by either McDonald or Mackenzie to have a watchdog committee composed of Members, as it is in the United States. A few years ago I would have opted for Members, without question. Now, as I approach the exalted status of being nothing more than a Privy Councillor, whenever the election occurs, my opinion of Privy Councillors is starting to go up. However, 1 do not want to be facetious. On balance, I believe I prefer the recommendation of the McDonald Commission. I regret that I am not on the particular committee that will be studying this, but I would be quite prepared to discuss the two alternatives at committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) a question. He has followed this entire issue as critic and now as a member of the Loyal Opposition responsible for this legislation. He has shown a great deal of interest in this particular legislation and knows full well how controversial and sensitive it has been. The questions which he has been asked today in terms of the content of his address have been basically directed to matters that can be dealt with in committee. In view of those facts and the fact that the security service now is basically in limbo as a result of the legislation being introduced and the uncertainty in view of the NDP's attitude toward the passage of this legislation, would he not agree that it is time that we proceeded to send this Bill to committee so that the matter can be dealt with there very thoroughly, and that the committee should take as much time as it requires to deal with all the specific items that are still controversial and need to be resolved?
Mr. Speaker, the short answer has to be no. I might comment that I am not responsible for our Party-
You should be.

The Minister says I should be. I should be the Minister of National Defence, but the fact is that I am not.
To deal seriously with what the Minister of National Defence puts to me, the short answer, regrettably, is no. The reason is that during 15 years-the Minister is well aware of this, having served as Solicitor General-there has not been public debate on this in the House. The only occasion was when the Mackenzie report was tabled. I believe the debate lasted either two hours or four hours.
The Government side may not like the quality of the debate. That is unfortunate. The quality of the contributions may not be of what it thinks are acceptable standards, but who are we to judge our colleagues? If there remains room for legitimate concern and for positive contributions at second reading stage,
Security Intelligence Service
then I do not believe that we should be in a hurry to send the Bill to committee. I emphasized the committee stage because I thought there was an enormous amount of work to do there. 1 think the Minister of National Defence implied in his question that he agrees that there is an enormous amount of work to do.
I will not use the usual vehicle of blaming the Government for holding off the legislation this long, but now we are at this stage I do not think I would tip my hand, were I the Solicitor General or a Member of the Government, by trying to push it through second reading stage too quickly. Often that results in its going more slowly than quickly. That has been my experience.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a number of comments have been made in the House regarding the committee stage and the fact that the committee should have the right to travel. As well, the Senate committee did hold extensive hearings but did not travel, which meant that only those who could afford to come here did so. Has the Hon. Member heard the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) indicate a willingness to have the committee travel?

Mr. Speaker, no, I have not heard the Solicitor General's opinion on that. I alluded to it during my contribution to the debate, perhaps too quickly. I merely thought it was absolutely essential that the committee travel. For example, those of us from Ontario are not sufficiently aware of the historic roots of the RCMP in western Canada to be as sensitive as we should. Taking the security service outside of the RCMP may cause fellow Canadians in other provinces, particularly in the West, grave concern. It may be an emotional concern. An emotional concern is a legitimate concern. I do not know how the committee can possibly discharge its responsibilities without being empowered to travel.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to add a few words of wisdom to the debate this afternoon on Bill C-9, the successive Bill to Bill C-157 that was dealt with in the last session of Parliament and gone over in some detail by the Senate committee.
When we look at the question with which we are faced today, namely the establishment of an independent Canadian Security Intelligence Service, we will see that there has been a gestation period of considerable length. The idea of a separate service and the idea of a specific Act of Parliament to control activities of a Security Intelligence Service goes back to sometime before the 1969 report of the Mackenzie Commission. It has been around that long. Very good recommendations were made on this subject by the McDonald Commission. I understand that it published its findings in 1981. There has been some debate in Parliament. It certainly has been a matter that has come up from time to time in Question Period. It has been on the minds of parliamentarians both in the House and the other place for some time. It has been a subject of comment in the press for a number of years. It has also been a matter of debate within the Department of Justice, within the interior works of Government, and I have known some of the people in the Department of Justice who have been involved in bringing

March 9, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
this legislation forth. I should like to compliment them on the work they have done in this regard.
While handing out compliments, I think some could be validly paid to our colleagues in the Senate whose committee did some excellent work on the old Bill C-157. We can thank them for the improved form that we have today.
As we debate this issue and study it, as public concerns are raised and debated, it seems that we are proceeding to some kind of general consensus on what type of Security and Intelligence Service would serve us best in Canada.
I would like to examine some of the issues, a non-exhaustive list of them but nevertheless issues which I would consider to be important ones which are addressed in this Bill, as they should be because they are certainly important when it comes to security work.
First, the security agency should operate under the rule of law. Unfortunately, this has not always been the case in the past, as the McDonald Commission has brought to light. Unfortunately, from time to time a security agency of the type that we envisage and of the type which exists presently in Canada and elsewhere in the world would have to do things that are normally outside of the law. So what we must build into the Bill, which I believe is there in large measure, although it will be examined again in committee, is some judicial control over actions which may become necessary in the best interests of Canada.
As I understand it, under this Act, if the security service would want to tap a telephone, open mail, or do any of these other things to which we have a natural repugnance but which may be necessary, it would have to seek judicial consent and get itself some kind of warrant. I hope that when such warrants are issued by some members of the judiciary they will not be blanket warrants. We do not want anything of the nature of a writ of assistance, which fortunately we are going to be rid of. Such warrants would give specific authority to do certain specific things within a certain specified time period. I hope that when judges are requested and give permission for these types of things to happen, they will be very cognizant of what they are doing and will be very careful and insist on having presented to them sufficient facts to justify the granting of such permission before they give that permission.
The second issue I would like to speak about briefly is the protection of the general public against possible abuse by the security service. In this imperfect world, even in a non-militaristic country like Canada-and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) knows how non-militaristic we are-there is a need for a security service. I hope it will be of a passive nature rather than an active nature, by which I mean that we would not go to other countries ferreting out their secrets. In other words, I hope it will operate within Canada and it will be a counter-espionage sort of organization instead of one that actively promotes espionage and related activities.
We need such a service, but it must not be allowed to get out of hand. I personally do not share in a paranoia of members of
the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker. I have a reasonable degree of confidence in officialdom in Canada. I know that often this is not a popular thing to say and that it is something that we on this side of the House very seldom say, but by and large the police in Canada, the existing security service within the RCMP, do a pretty good job, I think, and honest, law-abiding Canadians do not have much to fear from them. However, from time to time things do go wrong. There must be guidelines for the conduct of security officers laid down in the Act that is to govern them. There must be constant surveillance of the agents themselves to see they do not breach or use in excess the powers given to them. There must be a recourse for a person who feels he or she is wrongfully being investigated. Maybe they feel they have been harassed. There must be a recourse where they can go for a redress to their grievances. What we are saying here is that there must be a system of review.
I am pleased to see that a system of review is built into the Bill. It is a fairly sophisticated system of review. I hope that when this matter is studied in committee we can improve it even more, because it is of fundamental importance. One of the mechanisms for the protection of individuals in the Bill would be the establishment of the office of Inspector General. The Inspector General must have available to him or her full powers to question officers within the service. The Inspector General must have access to documents and files within the security service. He must not be impeded in any way from conducting his or her activities of supervising the security service. Maybe supervising is wrong because that is, of course, the responsibility of the director, but perhaps keeping tabs on the security service and keeping tabs on the director of the security service.
I personally like the idea of the Security Intelligence Review Committee. It is a very novel and interesting concept, having a committee of Privy Councillors who are not Members of Parliament either in this House or in the other place. It has never been tried before in this context or in other contexts as far as I know. It certainly has things to recommend it. I hope this is an idea that will be studied in detail in committee. We need to study the number, whether three or five or whatever number is sufficient. I am not adverse to trying out this idea of a committee of Privy Councillors to whom complaints can be made and who will receive the report of the Inspector General and report to Parliament on how the operation of the security service is going.
We must have built into the Bill accountability to Parliament. It must be the Minister who is accountable to Parliament. That goes without saying, Sir. I hope that parliamentarians will always have the opportunity to question the responsible Minister on the operations of the security service that reports to Parliament through him.
When we look at the review mechanisms that have been carefully incorporated into the Bill, the most important thing is that it will all depend upon the quality of the people who are appointed to these positions. We can be very, very careful on paper. It can seem like a system incapable of failure, but
March 9, 1984

unless we appoint the right people to the right jobs, then of course anything can fail, and no matter how well we draft the Bill, there is always the danger that the finer points of the law will not be kept and that it could slide downhill.
It will be most important who gets the job as director of the organization, who becomes the Inspector General and who makes up the committee. They will have to be people we can trust and 1 mean by that Canadians as a whole. They must be people in whom Canadians can have confidence. When I see some of the appointments that have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Members of his Government I have cause for concern. I get kind of scared as to who might get these jobs that are so important to Canadians. I am sure many other Canadians share that fear.
Another issue is that the NDP has made the right of dissent its sole and most important objection to this Bill. We in Canada have always enjoyed the right of dissent. As a Member of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, I am very jealous of the right of dissent and would not want it to disappear. It would accord hon. gentlemen opposite after the next election the same right of dissent which we on this side presently enjoy. The people of Canada must have and maintain the right to seek a change in government or a change in the social or economic order of Canada through peaceful and constitutional means. Of course they must not resort to subversion or go against the Constitution of Canada, but they must have the right to seek change through peaceful and constitutional means free of harassment by officialdom.
I would now like to refer to the principal issue in this Bill. It is the most important and most talked about by the man on the street. I am referring to whether or not we should have an independent security agency and not use the RCMP as we do at the present time. It was the recommendation of both Mackenzie and McDonald that there be an independent agency. In fact, most countries of the world have independent agencies. Of that there is no doubt. When talking to experts in this field, I have found that they invariably point out the basic difference between police work proper and security work. The latter, security work, is very much intelligence gathering as opposed to strictly law enforcement. I am pleased to see, however, that when it comes time for charges to be laid under the Official Secrets Act or perhaps under the Criminal Code, the RCMP will be brought in to do that, which is quite correctly police work. This is a proposal under the Bill.
Despite some bad examples, it is my opinion that the security service of the RCMP has done a pretty good job over the years. Therefore, there is no great and immediate urgency to change. It might be desirable that we do so, and I am quite prepared to discuss that. However, unlike the Minister of National Defence, I do not think it is something which has to be done today, tomorrow or a week hence. We could continue for a period of some time to debate this matter.
Then I come to the principal difficulty of getting this concept of an independent agency across to the public of
Security Intelligence Service
Canada. We have a Bill which makes a good deal of sense, if one chooses to read it. It is something which should be discussed and has considerable merit. However, the public of Canada just does not trust the present Government; it has no confidence in the present Government. However, it has confidence in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The public of Canada is used to the force and has generally received good service from it. That is not something which could be said about the Government. Therefore, any proposed change in security matters by the present Government of Canada is rejected out of hand by the Canadian population because of the distrust which exists. If we look at the horror stories in the Department of National Revenue, we know that the Government has lost control of that Department. We hope that it will never lose control of the security agency. If we look at the attitude of people within that Department of Government, if we look at the complaints system when citizens are ajudged to be guilty unless they can prove themselves to be innocent at great expense to themselves, when we see those types of things going wrong within a Government Department under the jurisdiction of the hon. gentleman opposite, then we cannot help but think that the people of Canada are reluctant to agree with any proposed change in security matters when the people over there still exist as the Government.
My conclusion therefore is that there are some very good points in the Bill. It deserves additional debate. I would like to see at least some of its recommendations come into force, but the timing is wrong because Canadians do not trust the Government which is in office today; they do not trust the Liberal Government. Before this Bill can be made into law and put into force with the consent of the Canadian public, we must change the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) a question. He went on at some length to express his confidence that any civilian Canadian security and intelligence agency would not exceed its bounds. Also he stated that some Canadians might be surprised at that statement. However, I must say that that statement was, to say the least, rather odd in view of the tremendous furor which he and his Conservative colleagues raised over what they called the recent covert activities of staff in the Office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in spying and engaging in "dirty tricks" investigations of Opposition politicians. Is he now saying that he and his colleagues at that time were just playing the game of Trivial Pursuit in the House? If that is not what he is saying, on what does he base his current statement of faith and confidence in the Government and its agencies that they will not tamper with the right of their legitimate political opposition, which his Party suggested was the case only a few days ago?
I do not share that kind of suspicion but I would suggest to him-and I hope he bears it in mind in his answer-that it is not enough to have confidence in the Government and its agencies in these kinds of areas in normal times. We must design our laws in such a way that if we get into abnormal times such as we did at the time of the so-called FLQ crisis, we

March 9, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
still have safeguards in the law to protect us from abuses which any government is tempted to commit in times of severe stress.
My main question to him is: Were they engaging in Trivial Pursuit just a few weeks ago? If not, on what does he base his current statement of faith in the activities of the Government and its agencies?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly did not say that I had any faith in the Government. If by that he meant the hon. gentlemen sitting on the Treasury benches, I have very little faith in them. What I said was that by and large I think we have a very competent and honest bureaucracy in Canada. Most people I have met during my daily rounds, both as a Member of Parliament and before coming to this House, whether they serve in the passport office or are employees of the Department of National Health and Welfare, try to do a good job for the people of Canada. It does not mean to say that there are not some exceptions. I went to considerable length in my dissertation this afternoon to point out that when it comes to police and security matters, there must be built into the legislation which governs the activities of these types of departments and agencies something more and something special so that the interests of the citizens to be able to engage in dissenting activities in order to press for change, political or otherwise, should not be hampered. I thought I dealt with that in great detail.
It would appear that my own view and that of the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) on this matter are not at all widely divergent. We would seem to be of very much one and the same mind on this issue.
I turn to the shenanigans to which the Hon. Member referred which were going on a week or so ago. These were conducted not by the ordinary government employee who is non-partisan and non-political and whose job is administration. These activities were engaged in by employees of the Prime Minister's Office, an office which is right at the top of the hierarchy. Unfortunately, we can see the rot setting in, and the rot is setting in from the top. I do not like or approve of the things that went on in the Prime Minister's Office, but I do not think that it is the normal, average bureaucrat, public servant in Canada, who is responsible for that type of insidious activity.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that some of the same rot that has set in must have seeped across the way to the offices of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney). Of course, the same kinds of files were found in his office, and in fact in much greater quantity.
I would like to ask a very straightforward question of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). Does the Hon. Member in fact support the recommendations of the McDonald Commission for a civilian security service as opposed to maintaining the security service within the structure of the RCMP?

Mr. Speaker, generally speaking, as I pointed out in my presentation, I approve of that move. However, as I was at great pains to point out, the timing is wrong because it is impossible to do this with the concurrence of the public when we have in office a Government that just cannot be trusted.

Mr. Speaker, I think I heard the Hon. Member say that the RCMP security service has done a pretty good job over the years. I put this question to the Hon. Member as someone who was a Crown Attorney, who has had many friends who belong to the RCMP and who has respected much of the work done in the general force. In view of the barn burning, the access to files of political Parties and the whole list of illegal acts which have taken place over the years, can the Hon. Member really say that the RCMP security service has done a pretty good job over the years? I put it to the Hon. Member that it seems to me that the acts of the RCMP security service have forced the McDonald Commission almost to succeed in destroying the RCMP-
And their political masters.

As my colleague has said, their political masters were involved in this matter as well. I wonder if the Hon. Member really does stand behind the statement that the security service has done a pretty good job over the years. It seems to me that if what went on in the last 10 years in Canada had occurred in the United States, there would have been a revolution against it. It would have been akin to a Watergate scandal, and yet nothing really happened in Canada. Does the Hon. member still stand behind that statement? If he does, it seems to me to be a pretty shallow analysis.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) that in Canada we do not have revolutions, we have royal commissions. It is a much safer way of dealing with things.
Undoubtedly, those things which took place in Quebec, including the barn burning and the surveillance of the Parti Quebecois, were not things that were to be desired. This is where the existing system fell down, and I suspect that it fell down because, in this particular case, undue political direction was given to the security branch of the RCMP. However, 1 still maintain that by and large, over the years, the RCMP has done a reasonable job.
I am not particularly familiar with what goes on in the Province of Quebec, but in my part of the country and other parts of western Canada that I visit from time to time, I very seldom hear complaints from people who have been subjected to abuse by the RCMP security agency. We just do not hear about these things. Apparently they do not happen.
Canada has not been brought to its knees by the activities of subversive agents. That means either that there have been no subversive agents working in Canada or that the RCMP has done a pretty good job and caught them all.
March 9, 1984

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The question period has expired. 1 would also like to remind Hon. Members that we are entering a new phase of debate during which Hon. Members' speeches will be limited to 10 minutes and there will be no question period, as provided for in our rules.
Mr. Speaker, I only have 10 minutes to make some remarks about this Bill so I will try to be brief.
That's a good idea.

1 have to be brief. I would like to make one comment about the attempt on the part of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) to stop this debate. I think that that is disgusting. We are finally having a debate on one of the most important issues in contemporary Canada, and they want to hustle it off to a committee which they can control and where they can effectively bury the Bill. Indeed, this week the Solicitor General has been running around the House like a rabbit in heat trying to have us shut up and get this Bill into committee.
It may be unpopular to speak on this Bill, but I would remind the House through you, Mr. Speaker, that some of us on this side of the House remember some very unpopular things which were said by our predecessors. J. S. Woodsworth stood in the House and defended Chinese immigration and argued, against the rest of the House, for the equal treatment of Chinese Canadians. One of my predecessors in the riding of Vancouver-Kingsway, Angus Maclnnis, stood up alone in the House against a tidal wave of opinion to defend Japanese Canadians. Grace Maclnnis, a previous Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, stood up and voted against the War Measures Act together with my other colleagues. That took courage and resistance, and those people were proven right in the long run. I think that some of the work the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has been doing regarding this Bill will serve Canada well as we will get a better security service for it.
There are four things wrong with this Bill, Mr. Speaker. First, there is no parliamentary accountability. Second, the group that is supposed to look at the security service is denied access to Cabinet documents, the kind of documents that are really needed in order to examine the service. Third, the powers of the service are too broad. Fourth, the mandate is too vague. That is what is wrong with the Bill, and that is why we must debate the Bill in principle on second reading.
Let me go over those four points briefly, starting with parliamentary accountability. I do not agree with the two previous speakers who said that it is all right to have a bunch of old Privy Councillors, some of whom are perhaps in their dotage, looking at the security service. It will be accountable to some, mainly Liberal, Privy Councillors, but that does not matter. Those Privy Councillors have probably retired from politics, so let us do it in a contemporary way. Let us put accountability where the United States does. Let us put it into the legislature. Let us have a parliamentary committee. That is why we have a Parliament. Parliament does not exist so that
Security Intelligence Service
former Privy Councillors may find jobs. Let us have a parliamentary committee that looks at the security service and really makes it accountable.
Second, we must see that that parliamentary committee has access to the same Cabinet documents to which the security service itself has access. We must deal with the type of access to information that the people who will keep the security service accountable will have.
Third, the powers are too broad. I ask Canadians who are watching these proceedings on television whether we want a security service to open up our first-class mail. Do they think that the danger of subversion in Canada is that bad? I do not think it is, and therefore I do not think a security service should have those broad powers.
Fourth, I think the mandate is too vague. My colleagues have said that this will open up the possibility of looking into legitimate groups, such as church groups, peace groups and so on, or even looking on the left and on the right. The Peter Worthingtons will be looked at just as much as the groups on the left. That is the history of what the security service has been doing in Canada. It is shown in the McDonald Commission. The evidence is there, Mr. Speaker.
The Solicitor General of Canada is a chicken. He has
800,000	files on average Canadians and he is afraid to tear up those files and get rid of them. What is he waiting for? If he had any guts, he would do that. He is a wishy-washy chicken. He has no guts to do that. Here he comes into the House now. He is gutless. He has been running around, but he should have been fired because of this Bill. He should have been fired for the way he brought in this Bill.
Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege.
You will get a chance to speak.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Minister rises on a question of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, I am astonished to hear the Hon. Member call me gutless on the grounds that he did. Naturally he is entitled to call me-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. There is no question of privilege. I have 10 minutes to speak.
-whatever he likes but the fact is-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. May I remind the hon. gentlemen that we cannot entertain a point of order on top of a question of privilege. We will hear the question of privilege first.
There is no question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask that the Hon. Member withdraw the allegation that I am gutless. He knows perfectly that that file destruction is well under way and that

March 9, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
hundreds of thousands of files have already been destroyed. I have reported that in the House.
May I see my file?
Can you read?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The Chair is of the opinion that the Hon. Solicitor General has made his point. Certainly the term used is not very polite, but I doubt whether it falls within the realm of unparliamentary language.
May I remind the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) that he may well continue his speech but he might try to make it a bit less inflammatory.

Mr. Speaker, let me just say that the Minister lacks intestinal fortitude.
Where is the proof? The Minister brought in a most flawed Bill. It is amazing that he was not fired because of it. He kept his job by getting Senator Pitfield to bail him out. The Bill is still flawed, and that is what we are trying to point out.
There is no mandate in the Bill that is defined properly. We can still have the point of opening files on Canadians; we can still have the point of looking into peace groups and other groups, and that has been pointed out by my colleagues in the House. There has been no real coming to grips with the crucial difference between dissent and surveillance. Indeed, that is the whole problem.
There are four points, then, Mr. Speaker. There is no parliamentary accountability; there is denial of access to the proper files to have that accountability; the powers are too broad in the Bill; and the mandate is too vague.
I have never seen the question of whether the country really needs a security service properly debated in the House, Mr. Speaker. The world has the FBI, the NKVD and its successor the KGB, and the RCMP security service. What are these groups really doing? I should like to suggest that they do not spend their time in surveillance of criminals and subversives. We have the Criminal Code for that in this country. We have the ordinary services of the police, but we have created these crazy bureaucracies that go out to do nothing but get files on people. That is why the debate is so important today.
I do not speak for my Party now, Mr. Speaker, because the views of this Party are quite clear; the Party is on record as wanting a security service but giving it a defined mandate. I raise the question of why we have security services at all? Is Canada really so insecure? Do we really have all these secrets that we need this kind of agency?
I should like to put something on the record, Mr. Speaker, which I think applies here. I read as follows:
It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen. Winston Smith, his chin nuzzled into his breast in an effort to escape the vile wind, slipped quickly through the glass doors of Victory Mansions, though not quickly enough to prevent a swirl of gritty dust from entering along with him.
In the next paragraph this appears:
The flat was seven flights up, and Winston, who was thirty-nine and had a varicose ulcer above his right ankle, went slowly, resting several times on the way. On each landing, opposite the lift-shaft, the poster with the enormous face gazed from the wall. It was one of those pictures which are so contrived that the eyes follow you about when you move. BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU, the caption beneath it ran.
That, of course, is from Orwell's 1984. We are in 1984-
Cheap shot.

It is not a cheap shot. The whole basis of the debate is how much we want to restrict Big Brother. If we want to make sure that Big Brother is not going to watch us and that we are not going to create that kind of society where we have a "Minister of Love," and so on-

Perhaps I could finish, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate briefly in the debate mainly because of my concern about one aspect of the procedure we are going through. The Bill was introduced first in the Senate as Bill C-157 and it received quite a thorough analysis in Ottawa by a committee of the Senate. The witnesses who appeared were those who could afford to come here and make their presentations.
A Bill to establish a security service has been discussed for 10 or 15 years. There were two royal commissions to study it, and then the Government introduced Bill C-157 in the Senate. That Bill was roundly criticized and partially condemned, and the Government withdrew it. Now it has introduced a revised version, taking into consideration many of the recommendations made in the Senate. The Bill has been modified, changed and vastly improved, but still I think there is room for more improvement.
Since the Bill has the potential of invading Joe Citizen's life in any corner of the country, has the potential to investigate political Parties and political activities, has the potential to look into areas that we would prefer to think were not being looked into, I think it must be considered very carefully and must receive a great deal of support from all Canadians.
I believe that there is no doubt that we need a security service. Every country has a form of service which tries to protect the way of life it has established. We have had one for some years. It has erred and has had problems from time to time, but by and large it has done some good work for us. To win overwhelming support for a security service, whether it be a civilian service or one within the RCMP, I think the committee must travel to various parts of the country and listen to citizens and groups and lobbying organizations which cannot afford to come to Ottawa, to the other Chamber with the red carpet. If we really want to understand average Joe Q citizen's
March 9, 1984

views, then the committee must have the right to travel. The Government has refused that request. It claims that while there is a Liberal leadership race going on, it must have its people in Ottawa because it is afraid it might be defeated in the House. I say to the Government that the committee could travel under certain conditions, such as that there would be an equal number of Members from both sides of the House on the committee. In that way the Government will be able to protect itself.
Do you agree not to defeat us in votes in the House while the committee is travelling?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I am suggesting that if you spoke to the House Leader and made a proposal that an equal number of Hon. Members from both sides who would be away would not vote and you would not be defeated because of that committee travelling, I believe that would be a fair thing to suggest. If Hon. Members opposite want to fold up shop and run around like everyone else, not because of that committee's work but because they do not like running the Government any more, or have found they cannot, then I believe that, yes, they deserve to be defeated. The Hon. Member who has already left the House-I hope he is not going to embark in debate from behind the curtain-believes, I feel, that this is a fair offer or suggestion. If the Government wanted to make sure it was not going to be defeated because of that committee's travelling, it could put forward a proposal to make sure the committee had the right to travel but that the Government itself was protected. I believe that is a fair suggestion. I feel we have to have this committee travel. The Government has refused, and I believe that is a mistake. This is far too important a piece of legislation.
I want to hear from more than the Attorneys General of the various provinces. I want to hear from more than the people who can afford to be in Ottawa, the spokespersons for organized groups which have sufficient funds to be able to send them here. I want to hear from the average person and from some of the groups who would not otherwise be able to make a representations in front of the committee. I do not like cutting off representations from the Canadian public. We are here to serve the public. This Bill has the possibility of intruding into the fabric of Canadian life, into the individual's life and into political life, although I am not saying it will do so. However, in looking at certain of the provisions in the Bill, some of which were accepted recommendations from the Senate, there is no doubt that the security service must walk a very narrow tightrope. It will not be comfortable because it may fall off- we hope not very often. I believe that since this is such a potentially intrusive device into the lives of Canadians individuals and legitimate organizations, we have to hear from any person who has that concern.
I feel it will serve the purposes of the Government as well, because the Government would have a chance to explain the real intent of this Bill and it would receive the support, I believe, of the majority of Canadians. If the Government
Security Intelligence Service
wants the support of Canadians for the Bill, why does it not go out and talk to Canadians and give them an opportunity for input?

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-9 is an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. I am a layman, Mr. Speaker, and the intricacies of this legislation, in great part, escape me, but I have listened with great interest to everything that has been said from this side of the House. I am a bit disappointed that there has not been more debate from the government side. However, I have great confidence in Hon. Members of this Party who will consider this Bill in great detail in committee. Indeed, I hope that the Government will take heed of what they have to say, because I firmly believe that this Bill is long overdue and that if it is a good Bill when it comes out of committee, it will indeed serve Canada well.
Bill C-9 is a culmination of the work of two commissions of inquiry, of the special committee of the Senate, and it follows Bill C-157. The first of the commissions of inquiry was the royal commission into security, which we know as the Mackenzie Commission. The report of this commission was tabled in 1969 and it was left to gather dust. In 1977 another royal commission was appointed. After four long years, the McDonald Commission created a response to occurrences of the 1970s and was, in great part, related to the activities of the FLQ in Quebec. The McDonald Commission reported in 1981, and following its mandate it made specific recommendations with respect to security matters.
The Government, realizing the importance of this matter, took two years to respond. In May of 1983 the Minister supported the first draft of Bill C-157. Bill C-157, as we know, Mr. Speaker, was a disaster. It was a disgrace in drafting. It certainly was not worthy of presentation. However, I do not share that view as far as Bill C-9 is concerned. The Bill deals with national security. I certainly cannot agree with one of the last speakers that national security is not something which we should worry about or that we should defend against in Canada. The Solicitor General, realizing that Bill C-157 was an impoverished attempt at creating a Security Intelligence Service, referred the matter to the chamber of sober second thought. I do believe that certain members of the Senate performed a yeoman's service in pointing out the fallacies of that piece of proposed legislation.
Specific changes recommended by the Senate committee were vast and far too numerous to go through item by item today. In general terms, Mr. Speaker, the committee attempted to rationalize the mandate of the proposed security service. The Senate committee saw the powers of the security service as being carelessly defined, that the powers were broad and they were ambiguous.
In response to the haphazard definition of the security services' powers, the committee attempted to define clearly what "threats to the security of Canada" were. Thus, there was the recommendation to have the words "strictly necessary" added. The mandate was limited from an overly expansive interpretation to a mandate which gave powers only if

March 9, 1984
Animal Traps
"strictly necessary" for the protection of Canada's security. Even in the present Bill there is much protection missing in terms of the tremendous power which any such force will have. Certainly, it is the obligation of this House to consider carefully the legislative proposals which will grant far-reaching powers to the security service; powers, if abused, which will counter all that our political system now stands for. If Canada is to have a security service, it had better define the powers which it will give members of any such force.
Another area of Bill C-157 which the Senate committee attempted to correct can be labelled as accountability. Accountability is a subject which the Government is not well versed in. Whether it be Crown corporations or the proposed security service, the Government seems to regard accountability as a hassle. In the old Bill, ministerial accountability was sadly, but not surprisingly, lacking. The Director of the service, an appointed official, would have prevailed over the Minister. Had Bill C-157 been adopted, Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) would not have been responsible to the elected representatives of the Canadian people for his actions. A lack of accountability of this nature is disturbing in any area of government, but it is reprehensible in an area of such importance.
Naturally, the Senate committee recommended a complete reversal of this lack of accountability. The committee recommended that the service be an "open book" to the Minister, who will consequently have full political responsibility for matters of which he can reasonably be expected to have knowledge.

subsubtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF RAIL LINES IN NORTHWEST SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The reason for putting this on the Order Paper is to try to come to grips with some of the problems of economic development in northwestern Saskatchewan. Since the days of the early fur trade when French and Scottish traders came through the waterways of northern Saskatchewan, the economic situation in that area has become increasingly worse. Traditionally, most of the people who live in that area relied on hunting, fishing and trapping for their livelihood. Their every day activities were an integral part of providing food and shelter for themselves. As time passed, these people found they could no longer rely on fishing, trapping and hunting to provide the every day necessities and a decent standard of living. We now find ourselves in a situation where almost every community in the area affected by this Bill has in excess of 90 per cent unemployment.
As I said to the former Minister of Transport, it also encompasses an area where 60 per cent or more of the population are Indian or Metis people who have not had the high standard of living other people have throughout Canada. I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mrs. Cote) to pay particular attention to what I am proposing, which is to have a committee or group within the Department of Transport look at the socio-economic
March 9, 1984

impact of building a railway in northern Saskatchewan. It would connect communities, such as La Loche, Buffalo Narrows, Beauval, Meadow Lake and south, with the main lines.
I do not know exactly how much this would cost because the Department of Transport does not know what the cost would be. I tried to look into this with the railway companies. However, it would certainly have an impact if the railway were to go ahead and connect those communities I mentioned. In the initial stages it would provide a good number of jobs for people in northern Saskatchewan during the construction phase. A second benefit is that once the line was in place there would be a cheap and economical means of transporting goods in and out of northern Saskatchewan, whether they be manufactured goods coming in or raw materials going out.
I have mentioned that many of the people have traditionally relied on fishing in that part of northern Saskatchewan. However, we find today that commercial fresh water fisheries are almost non-existent in many communities. That is because of the very high transportation costs of getting fish out of places like the Athabasca region and many other areas. By the time fish is taken to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation plant in Strathcona, in Winnipeg, the transportation costs have not only eaten up the profit, but in some cases there would be a loss by the time the fish is taken to the plant in Winnipeg. I cannot say that I would want a system of branch lines such as is necessary to serve the agricultural communities in Saskatchewan, but at least let us have one main line, with possibly marshalling facilities at La Loche and Buffalo Narrows, so that raw materials from the north could be gathered together and shipped out by cheap and economical means, mainly rail transportation. Right now the air transport costs are prohibitively high, especially in northern Saskatchewan where they use small planes.
Some people might say that the idea is absurd, that there is no need, rationale or precedent for having a railway built in the north. However, I ask those people to examine the other provinces in western Canada. British Columbia has a railway up to the Yukon. Alberta has a railway right into the Northwest Territories. In Saskatchewan the rail line stops around the 52nd or 53rd parallel, at the community of Meadow Lake. That is the northernmost rail line in Saskatchewan. Ontario has a railway which goes right up to Moosonee and Moose Factory on James Bay. Those places are much farther north than the area I speak about in northern Saskatchewan.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) mentioned the railway facilities in Manitoba which go up to Churchill, and the grain terminal there. More of our grain from Saskatchewan should be moving through that port than goes out of there right now.
Therefore, if you look at many of the other provinces, especially the larger ones, you will see that they all have railways reaching much farther north, as far as into the Territorial areas, than we do in Saskatchewan.
I think the real need for a railway in that area, Mr. Speaker, is illustrated by the necessity for economic development of the area. As I mentioned, the standard of living has been very low
Transport
in northern Saskatchewan in the past. In fact, until the early 1970s when the Department of Northern Saskatchewan was established, many of the luxuries we take for granted were non-existent in that part of the province. For example, you would find ten or twelve members of a family living in one-room houses. Water and sewer facilities in many of the communities were non-existent. There was no form of recognized municipal government in many of these communities. When the Department of Northern Saskatchewan was established, it had a responsibility as a geographic department. The one department took care of all services in northern Saskatchewan including education, health, transportation, hydroelectric power, etc. These all fell under the umbrella of the Department of Northern Saskatchewan. That department had many difficulties in its formative years. The new Government in Saskatchewan has seen fit to abolish the department. I think that is sad, even though the services of the Department of Northern Saskatchewan were only a little more expensive than delivering programs and services through the line departments located in Regina. In many of those communities today there is modern housing with water and sewer facilities. New schools were built, making it unnecessary for students to leave their home communities to continue their education in high school. There are health clinics in many of the northern communities now.
The infrastructure which people need for a decent standard of living is there, but the economic development is very much lacking. One of the reasons for this is that there is not a form of transportation available to get raw materials out and manufactured materials back in at a reasonable cost. Companies wishing to locate a mine in northern Saskatchewan, or to be involved in another kind of economic venture, cannot do so because the transportation costs are incredibly high. If the railway was there, perhaps the transportation costs would be reduced to such an extent as to give an incentive to companies to develop some of the vast resources contained in northern Saskatchewan.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) will take this proposal to the Department of Transport and that it will look at the socio-economic impact of such a project. I would ask them first to consult with the local communities. Instead of consultation with local people taking place in the remote areas of Canada, often orders seems to have been passed down from up high. Many problems can be overcome with local consultation. Local consultation on a program such as this would be very helpful so as to overcome some of the stumbling blocks.
I suspect that a railway in northern Saskatchewan linking the communities I have already mentioned, would be very advantageous. I do not know that for a fact, Mr. Speaker, because the people in northern Saskatchewan do not have the resources to do a socio-economic analysis of what would happen if a railroad were built in the north. This would cost more money and take more resources than I myself or the local people have the ability or time to put together. I believe the

March 9, 1984
Transport
Department of Transport has the mandate and responsibility to consider this as a concept which would work better than what is now in place there to alleviate the economic disparities in that area of Canada. If the Department of Transport would study this proposal and then point out to me and to the people of northwestern Saskatchewan valid reasons why a project like this could not proceed, we would honour that. If it can document reasons why a railway in northwestern Saskatchewan is not possible, we would like to opportunity to refute its arguments.
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport to present this idea to the Department. I am not playing a political game or trying to force the Department to go ahead with something. I am asking the Department to study the socio-economic impact of building a railway in northwestern Saskatchewan. Give us the opportunity to consider this to determine whether it would be of benefit to the country and, more particularly, to the people of northwestern Saskatchewan, who in many cases are in dire straits and want something to happen. If this will bring about better social and economic conditions, I plead with the Parliamentary Secretary to help us out in this instance.

For the last two years, Mr. Speaker, that Hon. Member and that Party did everything in the book to prevent the passage of the Western Grain Transportation Act, Bill C-155. You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, the antics they pulled off in the House over the last year in attempting to prevent the passage of Bill C-155. Today the Hon. Member has the gall to bring in this motion asking the Government to set up a committee to improve the railway transportation system in Saskatchewan. What was Bill C-155 all about? Why all the opposition? He now presents a motion asking the Government to set up a committee to give him rail transportation in Saskatchewan. That Act heralded a whole new era in expanding transportation options in the West, which is what he is asking for.
