While the Hon. Member is dreaming of some pie in the sky rail lines, this Government has already acted. I
March 9, 1984

might remind the Hon. Member that Saskatchewan has one of the best networks of highways of any province in Canada. Perhaps the solution to the problem he is trying to solve may not be a rail line but other modes of transportation, which I think he should consider. There are busses which run cheaply. There are air services that the Government provides to outlying communities. If he were to look at a more multimodal approach to helping the constituency in his area, he might get much further than he is today.
For almost a decade the federal and Saskatchewan Governments have co-operated in measures to assist in the development of northern Saskatchewan. We have made substantial progress, particularly in the improved level of community services and transportation. However, with a major reduction in resource development and the possibility that new resources will not be identified in the foreseeable future, both Governments are concerned as to the economic development opportunities which could now be available to the northern communities. To this end, the Government has proposed the development of a memorandum of understanding in northern economic development by mid-1984. I believe this should be of interest to the Hon. Member with respect to his motion. The agreement would essentially identify ways of improving the co-ordination and existing federal and provincial programs in northern Saskatchewan.
A subsidiary agreement is also proposed to support northern economic development. Under this initiative, three priority areas have been identified for possible implementation during 1984-85. One priority area is resource development and exports. This is something the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) stressed in his latest Budget.
Another priority area is strategic economic diversification, where initiatives are intended to develop service opportunities.
The third priority area seeks to improve the participation of native peoples, including residents of northern Saskatchewan, and the opportunities and benefits of economic development.
In keeping with our historic concern and involvement with transportation in the Athabasca region of northwestern Saskatchewan, the federal Government has directed its efforts toward maintaining transportation services as is economically feasible while meeting the immediate needs of the communities. These are the very communities to which the Hon. Member is referring.
This has involved extensive consultation with residents of the region as well as with the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Two principal options emerged. The first one was the winter road. Each year the Saskatchewan Government, as I mentioned, has been providing a winter road from Cluff Lake to Uranium City, thus linking this part of northern Saskatchewan with the rest of the provinces' highway network. Again I must stress that its highway network is second to none in Canada. The federal Government will be most happy to consider any reasonable, well-defined and well-justified proposal from the Saskatchewan Government. Until then, we understand that the Saskatchewan Government will maintain,
Transport
at least for the current year, a winter road from Cluff Lake to Uranium City.
The other principal option was the marine mode. One consideration for the federal Government was to restructure marine transportation services on the Athabasca system. Everyone will agree that the marine services were of much value in the past. Notwithstanding the fact that with the closing of Uranium City, traffic has reduced considerably, a marine service in some form remains most strategic in meeting the remaining communities' needs.
Based on cost analysis, the Government recommended establishing a marine terminal tug and barge service at Fitzgerald, on the Slave River in Alberta. This meant that the tug and barge service out of Fort McMurray would be discontinued, thus alleviating the need to maintain the dredging program for the Athabasca River. During the ensuring consultation with both the Province of Alberta and Saskatchewan, a general consensus was reached for the federal Government to build a new tug and barge docking facility near Fort MacKay in Alberta, north of Fort McMurray on the Athabasca River. With the choice of Fort MacKay as the new barge terminal, a six-year program of reducing dredging by Public Works Canada will go into effect between Fort MacKay and Lake Athabasca. The number of navigational aids will be reduced on the Athabasca River to conform to the decrease in marine activity.
This continuation of the federal Government's dredging and navigational aids program will significantly reduce the potential negative cost impact on most area residents. The tug and barge service out of Fort McMurray will be terminated, along with the dredging on the Athabasca River between Fort McMurray and Fort MacKay.
As announced on February 28, the federal Government believes that with the new marine transportation service out of Fort MacKay and with the provincial Government's support, the transportation cost to consignees will be minimized and regional economic development will be encouraged. Any savings to Transport Canada as a result of these changes will be available to develop other regional transportation facilities in the Athabasca system.
Traditionally, the federal Government has played a very active role in the development of rail transportation services in Canada's northern communities. However, the geographic location, sparse settlement and great distances between populated areas in northwestern Saskatchewan make this region a high cost area to service, based essentially on community needs. This precludes, at least at this time, the development of further rail links with the rest of the Saskatchewan rail system until the resource potential is clearly identified to justify such an undertaking. We do not need a committee to determine that. That has already been well established.
Of course, it would be possible to construct a railway from the end of the existing railway network to Athabasca or that vicinity. This line, approximately 600 kilometres long, would be extremely expensive to construct. At approximately $625,000 per kilometre, I think we must ask ourselves if the federal

March 9, 1984
Transport
Government and the people of Saskatchewan can afford those types of costs. It should not be forgotten that it would also be necessary to upgrade the existing railway network from Meadow Lake to Prince Albert. This is a distance of 166 kilometres at a cost of $300,000 per kilometre. Such a line would be justified only if there were proven mineral deposits, such as those at Pine Point, Alberta, or in the Flin Flon region. Without proven deposits and a market for these products, it would be pointless to consider further extension to the continental railway network, which is what the motion is requesting.
We must remember, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces also play an important role in providing intra-provincial or local transportation services to their residents. Needless to say, the federal Government wishes to see the residents of these northern Saskatchewan communities receive the most efficient and convenient transportation service possible.
I would like to sum up by pointing out that a great deal of effort has been expended and much more will be required to ensure that transportation services in northern areas are sufficient to meet the demands of those requiring them. The provision of rail services, like any other mode of transport, has to be considered in the light of freight and passenger demand, or the number of industries or other facilities that would benefit.
The Hon. Member did not outline to this Chamber whether he was more interested in passenger service for those northern outlying regions, or whether he was more interested in freight service. Again I would remind the Hon. -the pipeline that should have been built down the Mackenzie Valley, the part of the country I have the honour to represent, would have done the same thing for us there. It would have increased economic development. It would have provided jobs, and it would have helped the same type of population that he has in his area as would his proposed rail line in Saskatchewan. However, at the time the NDP would not give support to that proposal, excellent as it was. Tom Berger and his accomplices were going up and down the Mackenzie Valley trying to garner votes for the NDP. They were telling people they did not want economic development, they did not need transportation, they should live in the bush and in tents, they should set traps for a living and set nets and they were not going to be part of modern Canada. That is what the NDP was saying just a few years ago.
I am very pleased to see that the NDP members are now having a change of heart, at least the more advanced NDP members from Saskatchewan. Maybe the B.C. NDP is still way back in the 19th century where it always was.
I am going to support the Hon. Member, but I am also going to make an observation. I was in Saskatchewan not that long ago. Saskatchewan had an NDP Government then. It had an NDP Government for eons before that. That is what I was told. Why did the NDP Government of Saskatchewan, like British Columbia that has a provincial railway going to the north, like Alberta that developed the Alberta Resources Railway and like the Province of Ontario which has a railway going to the Hudson Bay area, not take the slightest bit of interest in transportation routes in the north of that province during the many years it was in office? That NDP Government shared in part of the Berger-NDP-B.C. mentality which did not want to do anything and did not care whether or not the people living in those areas starved to death. Anyway, as I have said I am very pleased there has been a change of heart.
I think it is an excellent idea to encourage transportation links such as proposed by the Hon. Member. In looking at the map of Saskatchewan and the adjoining part of the Province of Alberta, it would appear to me that there is a natural rail link
March 9, 1984

transportation route-a natural corridor-which links the existing railway at Meadow Lake to the existing railway at Waterways, Alberta. This line could go through, as the Hon. Member suggests, La Loche and Buffalo Narrows. It would not be that long or that expensive a line. It is not like building a line to Athabasca or to some place like that. But it would undoubtedly have a greatly beneficial effect on the people who live within that natural corridor route.
Like the Hon. Member, I would like to see a permanent transportation link into Cree Lake, and hopefully at some time into Lake Athabasca-maybe connecting Cree Lake up to Lake Athabasca. I would certainly like to see that happen, although maybe that will be a few years down the road.
Perhaps the existing rail link at Fort McMurray could be extended into Lake Athabasca. That might, of course, be on the Alberta side at the border, and my good friend would obviously like to see it on the Saskatchewan side of the border. However, if that were to take place, it would benefit the Lake Athabasca communities, such as Uranium City, Stony Rapids, and Fond du Lac. It would seem to me that the secret of being able to build a railway and make it operate profitably without too much cost to the taxpayer in the form of subsidization would be to have a sufficient volume of goods to carry on that railway. One needs lots of bulk cargo, such as coal or grain, or perhaps cargo freight with a little higher value, thus allowing one to charge higher freight rates. You need to have a good customer at the end of the line in order to justify being able to build it.
There are two good examples of this that spring to mind. The first is the railway that was built in the 1950s to connect Grimshaw, Alberta, with the lead-zinc deposits at Pine Point, Northwest Territories. That line could not have been financed had we not the mine at Pine Point that was a paying customer. But because that line was built, primarily to service the mine, it has also been extremely useful to farmers in northern Alberta and has encouraged the development of agriculture in the High Level area in the northern part of that province. It has been beneficial to the people in northern Alberta and in the southern Mackenzie Valley by way of general freight.
A similar situation exists in Manitoba where the railway was built into Lynn Lake to service the mines there and the people along the route. If a government is interested in benefiting the people by the construction of a railway in places like northern Saskatchewan, it should be encouraging the development of mineral resources, because grain cannot be grown there and there is not much chance of discovering oil, as I understand it, in the pre-Cambrian areas of northern Saskatchewan. It should really be looking for mineral deposits. Once again we come up against what hitherto has been the NDP policy of not encouraging mineral development. In fact, it does everything possible to discourage mineral development. This has been particularly true in northern Saskatchewan where they are mainly looking for uranium. The NDP more than anyone else has been against the nuclear industry in
Transport
Canada and the mining of uranium. It is slitting its own throat, so to speak. It goes against anything which will justify the construction of a railway. I am completely unable to undertand that.
However, with the election of an enlightened Government in the Province of Saskatchewan, that Party now appears to be pursuing a policy designed to promote resource development- oil and potash in the south and base metals in the north. What we need in northern Saskatchewan to develop rail transportation links is a finding of base metal, not one of uranium which is a high-valued commodity that can be flown out and dealt with in relatively small quantities. We would really like to have a base metal mine there. Then they would more or less have to put a railway into that area to ship out the finished concentrate.
I would like to comment upon the remarks of the former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport. I do not know whether he is in the House now. It is difficult to see him because he sits at the back. He used to be about two rows from the front, but now they have recognized his true worth on that side and have put him at the back where we can hardly see him.

He came up with some good ideas. He said that very often it is not justifiable to build a railway and that the same amount of money can be used to build many more roads. The Saskatchewan Government should be-and it is doing it to a certain extent-engaging in road construction to tie all these outlying communities into the mainstream of Saskatchewan life. He also looked at the wider interprovincial perspective, which I would like to do for a while. I was pleased with his announcement that a barge service was to be put in at Fort McKay. Originally it went from Fort McMurray, but now it will go from Fort McKay becuase the uranium mine at Uranium City has been closed down and it does not justify dredging the Athabasca River between Fort McMurray and Fort McKay. The original idea of NTCL and the Department of Transport was to haul freight going to Lake Athabasca all the way up to Hay River and all the way back down to Fort Smith, put it on a barge at Fort Fitzgerald and then take it into there. That was absolutely crazy, although it would have benefited my constituency to a certain extent. It was much more logical to go the Fort McKay route. I am pleased to see that we will have continued navigation on the Athabasca River for some time to come.
The Fort Fitzgerald alternative might not have been quite as crazy had the road about which there has been talk for many years been completed between Fort Vermilion, Alberta and Fort Smith, Northwest Territories. This would cut off many hundreds of miles into Fort Smith and hooking on to the Slave River waterway which gives access to both Lake Athabasca and Great Slave Lake. Eventually, in the years to come, I look forward to the construction of a major road network in that area. I would dearly like to see as the first step the completion

of a road through Wood Buffalo National Park linking Fort Vermilion to Fort Smith. However, this should go hand in hand with the construction of a road from Fort McMurray up to Fort Chipewyan, giving access to Fake Athabasca, and on to Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories. This is a road for which people in northern Alberta and in southern Northwest Territories have been pushing for many years. Each year they have a snowmobile parade for several hundreds of miles from Fort McMurray to Fort Smith to publicize the necessity of this road. Were this to be completed, it would benefit Alberta, Northwest Territories, the Province of Saskatchewan and the people living in northern Saskatchewan around the fringes of Lake Athabasca.
This is what I wanted to bring to the attention of the House this afternoon. I congratulate the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake for bringing forward such an interesting subject. I assure him that he has my complete support for his proposals.

subsubtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF RAIL LINES IN NORTHWEST SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have had the honour of rising in the House to speak in the capacity of Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, and I wish to take this opportunity to thank the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for letting me continue my work as a Member of Parliament in an area that is of great interest to me. In fact, economic development in the riding I represent in the House is very much dependent on transportation. Before speaking to the motion before the House today-the motion moved by the Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish)-I would like to say a few words about the exceptional work done by my predecessor, the Member for Park-dale-High Park (Mr. Flis), who has just commented on the motion. You will understand I certainly cannot share the views expressed by my colleague in the Official Opposition, the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), who ought to know, even if his party did not stay in power long enough for him to find out, that-I am thinking of his comments regarding the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park-Parliamentary Secretaries are appointed for a specific period. This may be one or two years, but the fact that one is no longer a Parliamentary Secretary certainly does not constitute a demotion, and at this point I wish to pay tribute to the work done by my predecessor, the Member for Parkdale-High Park, to whom I offer my sincere thanks, on behalf of all my colleagues.
To get back to the motion before the House today, which concerns the establishment of a Committee to study the feasibility of present or future options for railway transportation in northern Saskatchewan, I would point out that transportation links for isolated regions in Canada certainly deserve the attention of the Government.
In fact, we are focussing special attention, not only on developing Canada's large urban centres, but also on putting an end to the isolation of rural regions and Canada's North. The Hon. Member's motion is therefore entirely appropriate.
However, I feel there is a case for putting the issue of transportation in northern Saskatchewan within a broader context, in order to provide a general picture of the transportation services offered in northern regions in the Prairie Provinces, and of the options that could be considered for further improving the quality of service offered to users and, consequently, to the taxpayer.
In keeping with the terms of its mandate, Transport Canada has to make sure that every region of the country is serviced by a passenger and freight transport network that is dependable and adequate and which, above all, fills the needs of the population. But there is more to it than that. Mindful of the objectives set by the Canadian Government, Transport Canada must seek in every possible way to get closer co-operation from the other Government levels-the Government of Saskatchewan in this case.
Such co-operation is not expected only from the public sector, Mr. Speaker, because the federal Government seeks the support of the private sector which has a leading role to play in any endeavour undertaken to bolster the economy of Canada.
Now I should like to say a few words about the services of the Northern Transportation Company which were operational until last year in the Lake Athabasca region. Considering the losses reported by that Crown corporation in 1982- $800,000-no one could reasonably expect that corporation to continue to provide services when tonnage-and income-kept going down year in and year out. Still, the Government will certainly continue to provide services to that region and its residents.
Under a freight transport network restructuration program, the Canadian Government will soon begin the construction of a new wharf for tug boats and barges at Fort McKay and maintain its dredging and navigational aids maintenance services.
In the statement he made last February 28, the Minister of Transport made it quite clear that, once the new tug boat and barge service is operational, with the support of the Saskatchewan Government, the cost of transportation to the cosignatories would be reduced and the local economy would be given a strong boost.
In this context, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to remind the Hon. Member that Transport Canada, the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the communities concerned along the Athabaska system have decided to have consultations in this regard. These consultations are now under way, as is the restructuring program. In other words, the private sector will have a most important role to play in the near future to maintain the flow of supplies along the Athabaska road.
I was saying earlier that the transportation services in Northern Saskatchewan should extend beyond the borders of the region. From a geopolitical point of view, we see that the northern part of the Prairie Provinces is provided with a transportation network which dates back to 1929 when the Churchill line was built in Manitoba. This line was later
March 9, 1984

expanded with the Lynn Lake, Flin Flon and Osborne Lake branches.
In Alberta, the construction of the railroad owned by the Northern Alberta Railways and operating between Edmonton and Waterways did put an end to the isolation of the region. While this line is located in Alberta, the Northern Transportation Company Limited has during the last forty years provided the area with a barge and tug service in summer from Waterways, that is from Fort McMurray and Fort MacKay, to the communities around Lake Athabaska.
While the federal Government readily appreciates the Hon. Member's desire to have railway branches extend further North from Northern Saskatchewan, the profitability of such costly projects must first be established.
The Hon. Member belongs to a party which favours job creation, for which I congratulate him, the extension of social services and the expansion of our social network. This Government agrees with some of these principles, but it is obvious that, when he suggests investing considerable amounts, for instance in the building of questionable profitability, the Hon. Member's suggestion flies in the face of his own principles.
On the other hand, the Saskatchewan Government has not been idle, far from it! Just like the federal Government, it has a most important role to play in the economic development of the northern part of its province. For instance, to mention just a few of the most positive aspects of its transportation policy in this area, may I indicate that it is subsidizing this year to the tune of some $300,000 transportation by air of perishable goods to communities without year round access roads.
The Saskatchewan government has also maintained for the past several years in the Uranium City area a 190-kilometer long winter road at a cost of $400,000 per year.
If the Saskatchewan government were to make other proposals to its federal counterpart for the improvement of the road system in that area of the province, I am sure that my colleague, the Canadian Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) would favourably receive this kind of representations which are quite consistent with his policy of opening up the northern and rural areas towards the larger industrial and demographic centres.
As a matter of fact, both levels of government are meeting regularly to consider whatever action must be taken to develop the economic potential of Northern Saskatchewan; this spirit of co-operation, I am pleased to report, has already resulted in a number of successes, including an increased level of services and transport to the communities. In order to reduce the
Transport
impact of the closing of mining operations and the reduction in services, both governments are considering the possibility of signing a memorandum of agreement concerning the economic development of Northern Saskatchewan in mid-1984. It would identify the means to increase and improve federal and provincial programs in that area.
I would like to come back for a moment to the matter of extending the railway system to the north of the province, as suggested by my colleague from The Battlefords-Meadow Lake. The Canadian Government has never hesitated, when prompted by economic considerations, to promote the construction of rail lines. The best examples are the new Western Grain Transportation Act, which will enable the two major railways to invest some 16.5 billion in the economy over the next ten years. Those funds will be used not only to improve Canadian exports more or less substantially but also to create thousands of jobs in the primary and manufacturing sectors. Another example of the Canadian Government's involvement in railway transportation is the studies by the Transport Canada's Centre for Transport Development in support of studies for the construction of the new British Columbia Railway's line from Anzac, near Prince George, to Tumbler Ridge's coal basins.
Those two examples among others show the Canadian Government's determination to support, where needed, projects for the construction and restructuring of our railway system. However, Mr. Speaker, a rail line from Meadow Lake to Lake Athabasca would cost a minimum of $625,000 per kilometre, not including the improvements needed to the line section between Prince Albert and Meadow Lake, which would involve $300,000 per kilometre.
Such investments can only be warranted where important mineral deposits are to be found in the area served by the line. Surely, the Hon. Member will admit that committing that kind of money to a line such as he is advocating would ignore basic economic principles. I would like, however, to reassure the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker-
